utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody again. I was told that the Defence wants to raise something. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the translation of some exhibits which have been MFI'd have now been up-loaded into e-court. And with your permission, I would like to read which of those exhibits have now been up-loaded that were previously MFI'd. This is D165, D172, D178, D180, D186, D218, D230, D232, D233, D258, D259, and D292. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gajic. These exhibits are now in evidence and no longer MFI'd. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back. Again, I have to remind you that the affirmation still applies. Mr. McCloskey is continuing his examination-in-chief. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we left off in our chronology at what we call the tunnel attack which occurred in June the 23rd or 24th. And could we now go to D00062. It should be tab 80. And this is a 28 June report, this time from the BiH Army, from the Zepa group, in the name of, if we see the last page, Commander Colonel Avdo Palic. And I just want to call your attention to the first paragraph, where it says -- where it refers to an order of the deputy commander of the 28th Division, Srebrenica, Major Ramiz Becirovic. And remind us, who was the commander of the 28th Division at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the division was Naser Oric, but at this time either in late May or early June, Oric, as well as a number of his principal staff officers, left the enclave and were actually in Tuzla at the time the operation began. So the deputy commander of the division was, in fact, exercising control, and that is Major Becirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Avdo Palic in this is referencing a confidential document that was sent to him, and referring to it as dated 20 June 1995: "... on measures to be taken for the execution of sabotage actions aimed at inflicting losses upon the aggressor, in terms of troops and equipment, and, in general, at turning Chetnik forces away from Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the B/C/S version please be enlarged. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this related to the topic that you have discussed earlier, I believe, in connection to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Specifically, in May -- late April, actually, May and June of 1995, BiH military forces around Sarajevo launched a major offensive against the Bosnian Serb military forces encircling Sarajevo. One of the goals in other areas of the country was for other Bosnian Muslim military formations, to include the 28th Division, to conduct a series of attacks within their areas to prevent the Bosnian Serb military from pulling forces from other areas of the Republika Srpska and sending them to reinforce the Bosnian Serb positions around Sarajevo. So this particular document is a reflection of the operations taken by elements of the 28th Infantry Division, primarily those in Zepa, to conduct raids and other military operations in order to keep the surrounding Bosnian -- forces of the Bosnian Serb military surrounding Zepa in place there and not allow for the circumstances for them to be transferred to a more critical theatre of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know the command relationship between, well, Deputy Commander Becirovic in this case and commander of the Zepa forces, Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Palic was one of the subordinate commanders of the 28th Division. Zepa was physically separated from the Srebrenica enclave, but the Bosnian Muslim military unit in Zepa was considered to be a subordinate formation of the 28th Division. So even though Colonel Palic technically out-ranks Major Becirovic, by position Major Becirovic is in command because he is the division deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And continuing in the chronology, let's go to 65 ter 2091. And what we have here is a document from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a report to the president of the Republika Srpska. And if we flip through it, we see that it outlines the situation in the various corps and other information. Can you, just very briefly, tell us what you know about this kind of document? Not this one in particular, really, but what is this, this kind of report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is a report that the Main Staff did, I believe daily, to the president of the republic which laid out the general military situation within the Army of the Republika Srpska. It's actually the end report of a series of lines of where all the reporting goes. We've talked about earlier, for example, the brigade daily combat report. We've talked about the corps daily combat reports. Those reports, in turn, flow up to the Main Staff, which generates its own report to the president of the republic as well as to the corps commands, themselves, to lay out the country-wide picture so the entire army leadership, as well as the political leadership, has the view of the army as of what has happened today, what the current situation is, and what projected plans are for the next day or next period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see this is in the name of General Miletic. And if we could go to page 3 of this report in the English and the B/C/S, page 3, where we have the Drina Corps section, and we see, under "Situation in the Corps," the sentence: "Unengaged forces are being prepared for forthcoming active combat operations." So on 2 July 1995, what do you believe this is a reference to for the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of July, you see the first orders published by the Drina Corps to subordinate formations which discusses assembling military forces for what will be the Krivaja 95 operation, the attack on the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2091 shall be assigned Exhibit P2513. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we can now go to P1202, 82 in the tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we now have from the Command of the Drina Corps, dated 2 July 1995. At the end of it, it's under the commander, Major General Milenko Zivanovic, and it's entitled "Krivaja 95" in the top right-hand corner. We see that it's to the commands of various Drina Corps brigades. And then as it goes down, it's entitled "Order for Active Combat Activities, Operation 1." And just briefly, what is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the combat order to the various brigades that will send units or who will participate in the actual military operations at Srebrenica. It's a typical order that a corps would produce in this sense. It lays out what the enemy situation is. It lays out what the friendly situation is. It lays out, in general terms, first, what the tasks of the corps are and what the objectives will be, and then it starts to lay out the specific tasks for each unit, to include details of, you know, how they will advance, which axes of advance they will undertake. So, I mean, it's a relatively detailed document that is the work of the entire corps staff in order to produce and send down to subordinate formations, who will actually be engaged in the combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, would the Drina Corps had made the decision themselves to draw up plans and attack Srebrenica or would that have come from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision to do this would have been made at the Main Staff level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I think as you mentioned, the first part of this document talks about some of the enemy situations and where the enemy units are, so I'll -- that's self-explanatory. I'd like to go to page 3 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. It's -- number 2 is how it's numbered in the document, and it says: "The Command of the Drina Corps, pursuant to Operations Directive 7 and 7/1 of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and on the basis of the situation in the corps area of responsibility ..." And then it briefly mentions the task. But before we get to the task: Can you remind us, what does this Operations Directive 7 and 7/1?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the operations directives published in March of 1995 which, in part, laid out that the Drina Corps should engage in operations in order to physically separate the enclaves, and as noted in Directive 7, create the conditions for no further hope of survival within the context of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And as we go on, it says the corps: "... has the task of carrying out offensive activities with free forces deep in the Drina Corps zone, as soon as possible, in order to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica ..." And I'll stop there for now. Does that sound familiar, this "split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I just indicated that that was language that was incorporated in Directive 7 and 7/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your opinion, was this a legitimate military objective?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Limited to that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I believe you've talked about that before, so I won't ask you again about that. But did it have some relationship to what the Muslims were doing, as we saw in that other document, running sabotage operations outside the enclave to tie down troops?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then it goes on to say. "... split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, and to reduce them to their urban areas." What do you take that to mean, "reduce the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa to their urban areas"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the time of the creation of particularly the Srebrenica enclave, the actual boundaries of the enclave were never really clearly defined. By 1995, I think January or so, the Bosnian Serb military position, at least as articulated by General Zivanovic, the corps commander, on a number of occasions, was that the Bosnian Serbs felt that the actual enclave boundary for at least Srebrenica should be limited to the two- or three-square-kilometre area that encompassed the actual town of Srebrenica, and nothing further. So in this context, when you read that, they're again articulating their position that in their mind, the actual true boundaries of the enclaves are the urban areas of Srebrenica and, presumably, in the town of Zepa. They're not the much broader areas surrounding those towns, which is, in fact, where the military forces of the 28th Infantry Division are operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if one was to take military actions, offensive military actions, as it's described here, to reduce those borders, what effect would that have on the populations in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one assumes that the Bosnian Muslim population in the enclave would flee from the Bosnian Serb forces and fall back onto the town of Srebrenica, what you would have happen is, effectively, 30 -- 35.000, perhaps 40.000 civilians trying to crowd into that relatively small urban area. It would create essentially the same situation and humanitarian crisis that existed in Srebrenica in April of 1993 which caused the UN to have to declare the safe area in the first case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would the creation of this humanitarian situation you've talked about be consistent with what you just mentioned from Directive 7, creating an unbearable situation for the population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again taking the situation from 1993 as it existed, it was unbearable then, and it would have been unbearable again in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue to look at this. If we go to paragraph 4, we see a reiteration of the: "... separate the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica by attacking with a part of the free forces." And then it provides the actual trig points for the attack. And it also says under "Objective" on that same paragraph: "By a surprise attack, separate and reduce in size the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves to improve the tactical positions of the forces in the depth of the area, and to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves." I think we can understand that their tactical position would be improved if they took more ground, but can you tell us what you take this line to mean: "... and create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. When I read this particular document, my belief is that it articulates that the initial goal of Krivaja 1995, as laid out in this order, was not to capture the town of Srebrenica. It was, in fact, to create this humanitarian crisis, in a similar manner that existed in 1993, as a way to force the United Nations to come to the conclusion that the enclaves were not tenable and that it would be the United Nations that would evacuate the civilian population from the enclaves. Therefore, the Republika Srpska would achieve their particular objective and do so in such a way that they would not be blamed for ethnic cleansing. It would, in fact, be the United Nations that was withdrawing civilians from a combat zone. So when one looks at the limited scope of the order and how it does not include the actual capture of the towns, I believe that that is the most logical reading of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we note that this document, on the top right hand page, says "Strictly Confidential." How secret is such a command plan?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two classification levels within the Republika Srpska. "Strictly confidential" is the lower of the two levels. "State secret" is a higher level of classification. However, classified material was expected to be protected. Operation orders, particularly like this, would be of particular value for hostile forces to try and get ahold of so they could counter these operation. So, obviously, the fact that this, as well as most military documents, have a classification of "Strictly Confidential" reflects the fact that they are sensitive military documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could go to page 5 in the English. It should be page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I believe what I want to ask you about is the point that says "Task," and it says: "To be in readiness to launch an attack in order to strengthen the force and enhance the success along the battalion's axis of attacks; to repel an enemy counter-attack; to secure a hold on the features on the lines reached; and to prevent an enemy withdrawal." Which unit had this task?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can tell in the order, the designated reserve forces, which consisted of two or three companies of the MUP and one company from the Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade, had that particular task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to page 6 in the English. It should be paragraph 9, sorry, in the document. It may be B/C/S page 3 or 4, but it's numbered paragraph 9. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see that under "Anti-Airborne Landing Combat," that it says: "If NATO forces make an airborne landing in support of UNPROFOR, the units closest to the landing place and reserve forces will engage in combat with them." What's that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of the planning process, that at least the Drina Corps Command held open the possibility that NATO forces might seek to intervene in the upcoming military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did NATO troops ever intervene in the upcoming operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not ground troops, per se. However, there was NATO aircraft involved in operations against the Bosnian Serb military units. I believe those were on the morning or early afternoon of 11 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now we come to the section of the report, paragraph 10, which says "Combat Security," and A is "Intelligence Security." And if we go to page 7 in the English. I think we're still okay for the B/C/S. We see that B is under "Security," and it says: "Secure the complete secrecy of the decision and preparation for the execution of the task." Does that fit the definition and the proper role of the security branches in a combat report and in an actual combat operation, as you've defined and helped remind us of those rules and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we need to go to the next page in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see, in the English, as we go down a bit, it talks about coding documents, and then it says: "Security organs and military police will indicate the areas for gathering and securing prisoners of war and war booty." So here we have, in one sentence, the security organs, with the military police, and indicating areas for securing POWs. Can you tell us how that should work, under the rules? Well, is this according to the rules? And then, practically, how this should work on the ground.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is, first, in accordance with the established rules. In a more practical sense, it would entail brigade security officers working with the military police to identify and designate locations - they could be buildings, they just could be an open patch of field - where they would hold prisoners of war that were taken during the operation. Obviously, these locations would then be, you know, provided to subordinate formations. So as prisoners were captured, these subordinate formations could either bring the prisoners to that location or, perhaps, a process put in place where the military police would go down to that lower formation that captured the individual and return him to that designated location. Those are the types of procedures that it would be normal for the security officer and the military police to work out in advance of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Under a normal military situation, would the responsibilities of the security branch and the military police end there or would they normally involve further actions, proposals, anything?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. There would -- as part of the larger security and intelligence function, there should be plans made whereas intelligence officials would interrogate prisoners as they're being captured in order to obtain relevant battle-field information that could be of value to Bosnian Serb military forces as they continue the operation. You would also have a more sustained mission of guarding and securing the prisoners of war. You would be working, obviously, through the organs of the commander of the unit with respect to providing food, medical care, things of that nature, water, other forms of life support, and at some juncture you would either be transporting them back to -- further to the rear, towards a designated location, or other authorities who have been designated will come and pick the prisoners up from you and relieve you of that responsibility. Again, all of these types of activities would normally be planned in advance of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document in the chronology. It's 65 ter 2097. It's another Main Staff report to the president, dated 6th of July. And if we could just go to page 3 in the B/C/S and page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's, again, in the name of General Miletic. And looking at this situation in the corps, at page 3 in the B/C/S, page 4 in the English, it says: "The units of the corps stand are at the required level of combat readiness. The forces have been prepared and grouped for active combat operations towards the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa. Upon receiving an interim report, we will inform you on the combat results achieved so far." Can you explain how this reporting is working.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. While Main Staff is making this report, initially on a daily basis, it's recognised that as the combat operations begin, which they do on this day, that the situation will be changing with some fluidity. What is normally the procedure within the VRS is that while they will -- units will always do a daily combat report, when there is a change of circumstance or when the situation otherwise warrants, they will put out what's known as an interim combat report covering a shorter period of time or to discuss a more discrete battle-field activity that's affecting the unit. So at this juncture, everyone recognises that the operation is starting, and this is the Main Staff informing the consumers of this particular report, which would include the president, that they are awaiting additional reporting in the form of an interim combat report from the Drina Corps so they can start reporting up the chain the initial results of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, does the OTP have an interim report from the Main Staff to the president?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe so, sir. I don't recall seeing one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think everyone's familiar that the Drina Corps archives was obtained, at least in part. Are you aware of the OTP ever obtaining the collection of the Main Staff archives or the archives of the president of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, not that I'm aware of. Those -- in the case of the Drina Corps, those particular archives were accessed after my departure from this institution. So while I've seen some of the material relevant to it, I don't recall that I ever have a full accounting of everything that was in it. Again, I'm not aware of any Main Staff archives or presidential archives in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber has seen many documents from the Zvornik Brigade and the Bratunac Brigade. Did you have access to more complete collections of those materials?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Those particular documents, the Zvornik Brigade and Bratunac Brigade collections, were obtained by the Office of the Prosecutor during my period of service here, so, obviously, I had full access to that material. And that material makes up a large part of the foundations of my command reports and my narrative reports relating to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2097 shall be assigned Exhibit P2514. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to D00052.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as that's coming up: This is from the Bosnian Muslim army, the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this time the 2nd Corps Command out of Tuzla, dated 8 July 1995, and it's in the name of the commander, Brigadier Sead Delic. Now, we've seen -- you've discussed two other Muslim documents from the lower-level units, Srebrenica and Zepa. I just call your attention to the first paragraph, where, in the middle of it, it talks about the 28th Ground Army Division located in Srebrenica and Zepa, and that although completely encircled and facing big problems relating to survival and the obligation to protect territory, decided to contribute as much as possible to the fight against the aggressor, and stepped up their activities deep in the PZT. And then it goes on to describe the additional reason for the activities of the members of the 28th Division was to prevent enemy forces from sending additional troops to the Sarajevo theatre of operations from the area around Srebrenica and Zepa. And then it describes how; by causing losses, primarily the loss of manpower, which will force the aggressor to tie up troops in the wider area of Srebrenica and Zepa. Is this the same thing you've been talking about before, but just at a higher level, from a general of the 2nd Corps of the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you review these sorts of documents, and the intentions, and the situation in the Muslim army as part of your review in your reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, but to a far less degree than I reviewed that of the Bosnian Serb military forces. I reviewed and have some knowledge of the 28th Infantry Division documents in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor, because as part of my narrative reports, it was necessary to lay out, to at least a limited degree, the military forces that were operating in and around the enclaves from the Bosnian Muslim perspective. However, given what the goals and objectives of my reports were, which primarily focused on the activities of the Army of the Republika Srpska and how they related to the larger crime base of Srebrenica, what the 28th Infantry Division was doing up to the period of 10 July 1995 was not a particularly relevant part of that. Where it becomes more important, in the sense of the crime base, is what happens to the 28th Infantry Division and the accompanying civilians after the 10th of July, when they make the decision to withdraw from Srebrenica and form a column which then attempts to make its way from the former enclave to ABiH territory around Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue the chronology, and I'm hoping we'll get to July 13th by today, July 13th. But let's start with D69.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see here that this is from the Drina Corps Command to the now familiar General Zivanovic, 8 July, "Urgent," to the Pribicevac IKM, forward command post, Chief of Staff Krstic personally, and the GS VRS Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, to Major General Zdravko Tolimir, for information. And just looking at this first paragraph, it talks about: "The UNPROFOR Command in Sarajevo has filed a protest note with the Main Staff over operations against UNPROFOR observation points," listing them near Zeleni Jadar. As far as you know, briefly, did -- were there VRS operations against UNPROFOR observation posts in Zeleni Jadar on this date, in and around 8 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. From, actually, the beginning of the operation and moving forward, the VRS forces engaged in the attack knew that they would encounter the UN observation posts. And in a very similar manner to how they took down Observation Post Echo in May of 1995, they engaged in a similar tactic of firing close to or around the UN observation posts, without directly engaging them, in an effort to coerce the UN forces at those posts to deem the situation to be too dangerous for them to remain and for them to ultimately withdraw. In some cases, as part of this, the UN -- the personnel manning the UN observation posts fell back towards Srebrenica. In other instances, they placed themselves in the custody of the advancing soldiers of the VRS and were taken to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And since you're telling that part of it: Did the Dutch suffer any casualties in this process?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe on the 9th of July, one Dutch soldier was killed. However, in that particular instance he was not killed by fire from the VRS side. In fact, he was killed from fire by the Bosnian Muslim military forces. The UN found themselves in the middle in that particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what explanation do you have for the Muslim forces attacking the UN forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When that issue was investigated by the Dutch, initially, and others, the story that came out related to that was that a particular Bosnian Muslim soldier and members of their unit became frustrated that, in their opinion, the United Nations forces were not vigorously defending the positions against the advance of the Bosnian Serb army. So out of frustration, one particular soldier threw a grenade at a UN armoured personnel carrier, which, in turn, caused shrapnel injuries and the ultimate death of a Dutch soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get back to the document. We've mentioned that UNPROFOR had complained to the Main Staff about attacks on the observation point, and then this statement: "The Main Staff of the VRS answered that the Drina Corps Command had informed it that the Muslims were using six armoured personnel carriers, painted white and bearing UNPROFOR markings, and that the Muslims had started offensive operations from Srebrenica in order to join up the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa." Have you or the investigation found any indication that the Muslims had six armoured personnel carriers, painted white, bearing UN markings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. This is clearly a situation where a cover story, or disinformation, if you will, is being laid out so the Republika Srpska side has what they believe to be an adequate counter-argument to complaints by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Zivanovic goes on to say, among other things, that: "The Main Staff has ordered you not to attack UNPROFOR, but to prevent any surprises and stop the Muslims in their intention to join up Srebrenica and Zepa." What do you make of this order or reference to "has ordered you"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a reminder by the corps commander, General Zivanovic, to General Krstic, who is the chief of staff and actually running the operation at the time, that not -- his mission is not to become fixated with dealing with the UNPROFOR, but that he's to continue on his military mission, reminding him again that the UNPROFOR is not the objective of the military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we then see this comment: "Good luck in war, and best regards from General Tolimir." And as noted previously, this is sent to General Tolimir for his information at the Main Staff. What can you make of anything -- of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reading this document in its context, it's evident that General Tolimir had contacted General Zivanovic at some prior point and laid out what the Main Staff was hearing and had laid out the complaints that the UNPROFOR Command in Sarajevo were making, i.e., that protest note from -- you know, to the Main Staff of the VRS. So in General Zivanovic's response, he again lays all that out. It is sent to his subordinate commander, General Krstic, and an information copy is sent back up to General Tolimir so that General Tolimir is aware that General Zivanovic has acted upon the instructions and that all three of these general officers are fully aware of what was said, what the object of the document was. So it's a good example of how these senior-level officers of the VRS communicate with each other, and how they are making sure that, you know, their understanding of the objectives, goals and techniques of a particular issue are going to occur, and how they're all going to synchronise their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, this next document does not -- had not had a 65 ter number. We have marked it as 7254. It's one of the reports from Vujadin Popovic, so I would ask the Defence if they had any objections to its use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I welcome everyone present, the Prosecutor, Witness Butler and the Trial Chamber. May today end in keeping with God's will. The Defence does not mind the use of any document that could help establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document may be added to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General Tolimir. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Butler, this is a document, as we can see, from Lieutenant Colonel Vujadin Popovic, who we're now familiar with. It says it's from the Drina Corps Command, the Intelligence and Security Department, dated 9 July, to the VRS Main Staff, Security -- OB Sector, Security Administration, General Tolimir personally. And I won't get into all the observation in it. We can see the references to Zeleni Jadar and UNPROFOR forces pulling out from the check-points. And there is a statement here that -- taken by the Serb forces of one of the Dutch people which gets reproduced here. And if we go to the second page in the English, there's a note that the Muslim forces did not allow UNPROFOR to withdraw, and a reference to the Dutch gunner that was hit by Muslim fire and that his life could not be saved. Is this the reference -- is this the incident you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it mentions also that General Krstic sent a message out, through the communications channel, to the Dutch that if they felt threatened, they could safely withdraw to Serbian territory. I think we need to go to the next page in the Serbian. Perhaps not. It gets a bit cut off. There should be a list -- a clear list. Maybe it's on the previous page, a list of seven soldiers. There it is, yeah. And it makes a mention of: "After interview, the members of the observation posts were accommodated at the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac, and their personnel carrier was put on the grounds of the Bratunac Brigade." Are you aware of anything, from your review of documents or the materials or the investigation, whether or not, indeed, there were a number of Dutch soldiers that left their observation posts and were taken to the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think at one point, by the 11th of July, there are, perhaps, 20, 25 Dutch soldiers that are ultimately held at the Hotel Fontana. That number might even be a bit higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And at the end, it says: "We recommend that the VRS Main Staff take over further work and contacts with the Dutch Battalion Command by dispatching a liaison officer." Do you have anything to connect this proposal for a liaison officer with any officer that was dispatched to the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, initially the most immediate candidate for that would be Colonel Jankovic, who starts to become visible on the 11th of July, 1995. One will notice his physical presence in meetings with members of the Dutch that the VRS undertakes with General Mladic. So, I mean, he was the first person that I would see as a candidate from the Main Staff, based on the timing of when he appears on the -- in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "becomes visible," have you actually seen video of him at the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in that same video, do you recall whether or not there were Dutch soldiers shot and appeared on the video at Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume when you say "Dutch soldiers shot," you're basic saying appear on camera, as not physically shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Shot by cameras, yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, on those same video clips, Dutch soldiers are present at the Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again, very briefly, because I know we've got to get through, but does this fit within Vujadin Popovic's ambit, to be reporting this kind of material personally to General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again, just give us the brief outline of what it is in here that has to do with security and intel, in your view.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, from an intelligence perspective, the statement that at that point the only UN casualty that had occurred was a result of Muslim attacks, versus Serbian attacks, would be a valuable piece of information for the Main Staff to be aware of and be able to report back to the UNPROFOR Sarajevo as part of proof that, in fact, it was not the Bosnian Serb side attacking the UN, it was the Bosnian Muslim side. The Main Staff would certainly want to have a list of names of Dutch soldiers who were in their custody to, again, be able to provide that information to the UNPROFOR Sarajevo. So in the classic intelligence and security sense, these -- this type of information is an excellent example of the type of technical information that gets passed up and down the security chain to assist in facilitating the overall operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you recall, were these Dutch soldiers allowed to go back to their base after they arrived in Bratunac, where all the other Dutch soldiers were in Potocari, some - what? - five kilometres down the road?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not immediately, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were there, as -- the investigation, if you recall, revealed any threats against their lives by anyone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. On 11 July 1995, shortly after the first two NATO aircraft dropped bombs near the advancing VRS soldiers coming in towards Srebrenica, the Dutch indicate that over the UN radio network, they received a threat that they understand was delivered directly by General Mladic that indicated that if the NATO bombing did not stop, that Dutch soldiers would be harmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7254 shall be assigned Exhibit P2515. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to P590.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are still on July 9th, but we have a report from the Drina Corps forward command post at Pribicevac, "Very Urgent," to the Main Staff and the Drina Corps Command, entitled "Interim Combat Report." And we see it's in the name of Chief of Staff General Krstic. And there is a received stamp of "2320 hours." And from this, we can see a report on the combat and the features mentioned. And then, number 3: "Decision for further operations: Taking advantage of the success achieved, regroup the forces and carry out a vigorous and decisive attack towards Srebrenica." Then it mentions the surrendering of some UNPROFOR folks to the VRS, and a bit more discussion about UNPROFOR and check-points. Can you -- what do you make of this -- of this document, especially in relation to what you've said already occurred on July 9th at higher levels by the higher command? And if you can remind us of what you've said about that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What begins to happen on the 9th of July is that the VRS, themselves, are -- not only are they achieving their military objectives, their first limited military objectives, to advance and narrow down the enclaves, but they are beginning to realise that given the lack of a coherent defence, that for the first time they might actually have the military ability to capture the town of Srebrenica. So what starts to happen on the 9th of July is a series of discussions from corps to the Main Staff that ultimately reach the highest level, the president of the Republika Srpska, where President Karadzic, as the supreme commander, authorises the army to physically capture the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And at the bottom of paragraph 4, we see a note that: "UNPROFOR forces from the base in Potocari village did not intervene at the check-points or attack our forces." Did the behaviour of the UNPROFOR in this regard have anything to do with this pending decision to further the attack, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The fact that UNPROFOR would not vigorously defend the boundaries of the safe area or their positions, and the fact that to that point, the 28th Infantry Division was not able to provide for a coherent defence, bolstered the idea in the mind of the VRS that they could militarily take the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't want to spend a lot of time on this, but can -- realistically, militarily, would the Dutch soldiers and their equipment and the observation posts around the enclave, would they realistically be able to defend from this major attack by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: An interesting judgement question. In isolation, they had the equipment and personnel and the training to make a fight of it. They are the modern army. Even under the circumstances of reduced strength and limited ammunition, they certainly could have caused casualties among the approaching VRS forces. Coupled with operations with NATO air power, which would have acted as a significant force multiplier, it's entirely conceivable that they would have been able to stop the VRS in their tracks. But a decision to do so would have to be coupled with a political decision that you would accept the necessary casualties to do that and, at a broader political level, accept the fact that the UNPROFOR would completely lose any cover of neutrality that it still possessed by then, at least as far as the Bosnian Serbs would be concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So here we are on the 9th. The fighting is fierce. UNPROFOR is surrendering. You say there's no air power until the 11th. After the few bombs that were bombed on the 11th, and the threat went out about the Dutch hostages, did any other air power come in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just to be clear, the air power was available prior to the 11th. The air power was always available. A decision wasn't made by the UN to avail themselves to using NATO air power until the late evening of the 10th. And once the threat was made after the first strikes on the afternoon of the 11th against the Dutch soldiers, the United Nations immediately withdrew the option of using NATO air. So that pretty much ended any potential opportunity at that time of the UN defending the enclave even at that late stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So without air power, or, as you've said, without the willingness to use air power or ability to use it on the 9th/10th, what chance did the soldiers in the observation post have against the forces coming at them if they tried to fight them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can really say about that is it would have been -- it would have been a fight, it would have been a stubborn fight. The abstract variables, quite simply, that would have determined the fight would revolve around how many casualties the VRS would have been prepared to take from the Dutch in order to achieve their military objectives versus how many Dutch casualties they would have been willing to accept in defending the enclave. There certainly would have been significant casualties on both sides, given the context of close combat. But I guess it's just one of those unknowables of history to be able to say the Dutch could have prevailed or that they would have been defeated regardless. I just don't know the answer to that. I don't know that anyone can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 27 of today's transcript, lines 19 to about 25, you are making a reference to air power was available prior to the 11th, and the air power was always available. Do I understand those words to mean if the UNPROFOR had wanted, they could have called upon NATO at any time to come to their aid? That is the first question. The second is: You state again the United Nations did not avail themselves of NATO power, and once the United Nations -- sorry. Ultimately, the United Nations withdrew their option for using NATO air. Do you have -- can you assist? You may not have an opinion, but do you have an opinion as to why, ultimately, the United Nations did not want to avail themselves of NATO power and withdrew it at the point that they did? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In answer to your first question, ma'am, yes, they did have ability of NATO air power. While my opinion on the issue, I don't know that it is relevant, what I would offer is that the United Nations' own report on the fall of Srebrenica, which is included in its entirety as part of my narrative reports and I reference them, lays out in great detail the linkage between the United Nations forces on the ground and their ability to call upon NATO for additional air support when United Nations forces were at threat, and this particular document lays out the thresholds of the use. And, again, because it's a historical document, it also lays out in what I find to be excellent detail the decision process that went on between the UNPROFOR staff in Sarajevo, the UN Command in Zagreb, as well as other players in that decision, to include the Dutch government, in the decision on when to use air power and when to withdraw or when to stop using that air power. So my best answer to that would be: I would refer you to the United Nations' own report, and I believe they can give you the answers to those questions in far better detail than I can recall them at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'm not sure it's so clear, but if you'd answered -- the second question that Judge Nyambe asked is: In your view, why did the air power stop after the few bombs that you had mentioned hitting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, and I believe this is also referenced in various reports, it was a direct result of the threat that the VRS made to the Dutch soldiers who they were holding at the time in the Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for your information, the UN report is P1226 MFI only, and it is a large report. Mr. Butler does cite it repeatedly, and I would make it available and offer it into evidence at this time. And, of course, I can discuss this with the Defence to see if -- their view on that and see if there's -- perhaps it could be narrowed down. But I will get back to you on that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We can ask the Defence if there is any objection to that. Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Aleksandar will present our views on that. I would say we should not narrow down the evidence and then throw out what we want or don't want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the report of the Secretary-General, called "The Fall of Srebrenica" - I believe that is the document discussed by the witness - is already in evidence, and I would take the liberty of checking during the break under which number. I believe it has a D number, and I think the entire report is already in evidence. It was admitted a long time ago, in the first or the second month of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. It should be checked and reviewed during the break. Indeed, this is a good proposal. We are at the time of the first break, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I see you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I owe you one piece of information. The report of the Secretary-General, according to resolution of the General Assembly number 53/35, under the title "The Fall of Srebrenica," is Defence Exhibit D122. I'm sorry I said it was admitted in the first or the second month of the trial, but it was another report of the Dutch Army. This one was admitted a bit later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was not very mislead be, Mr. Gajic. Thank you very much for that clarification. And I take it that it is the same document as P1226 MFI'd. If that is the case, the latter one should be vacated by the Registry so that we have not -- this not in evidence twice.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the surrogate sheet will be up-loaded in e-court with appropriate cross-referencing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. And I have also been reminded, and I would remind the Court, that for the actual direct evidence related to the issue, we need to go way back for the review of General Nicolai's testimony, Major Franken's testimony on these topics, where they spoke from very close knowledge. All right. If we can now go to D41.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is, we will see, a now familiar document from the Main Staff of the VRS, "Very Urgent," to the president of the Republika Srpska and, for information, the Drina Corps IKM, Generals Gvero and Krstic personally. And is this a document that you have made reference to earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Several days ago, when I was asked a question as to what was the basis of my awareness that on the 9th of July, General Gvero was physically located at the Drina Corps forward command post, IKM, this was the document I had in mind which reflects the evidence that states that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just tell us what you mean? We see this is from General Tolimir. What is it about this, in particular, that leads you to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is copied to the president of the Republika Srpska for information, but the primary document is sent to the Drina Corps IKM, and it specifically says General Gvero and Krstic personally. Given the fact that it is General Tolimir sending this message, it reflects an awareness on General Tolimir's part as to where General Gvero is physically located at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see that it's entitled "Conduct of Combat Operations Around Srebrenica." And, again, I won't read all of it, but it notes that the president has been informed of successful combat operations around Srebrenica, and that they've achieved results which enable them to occupy the very town of Srebrenica. Has this changed from the directive -- what we saw, Directive 7, and then what we saw in the Krivaja attack plan?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It significantly changes the objective to now, for the first time, include the occupation of the town of Srebrenica by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And would this document that we can see that -- the referencing by General Tolimir, the president being informed of the conduct of operations and the president's decision, would this be along a normal chain of command and functions, as you understand it, or is there something odd or unusual about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. This is what I would consider to be a normal application of both the political and military chain of command, insomuch that President Karadzic is the supreme commander and that a decision relating to the actual capture or occupation of the town of Srebrenica would be one that, you know, he would logically be asked to agree with and give the order of such the military would propose, and obviously in this situation the military laid out the case that they had the ability take the town, that the military resistance [Realtime transcript read in error "assistance"] being offered was not countering that ability, and recognising that it's more than a military decision to take the town due to the various political ramifications. And that decision ultimately was made by the president of the Republika Srpska, wearing his hat as the supreme commander of the armed force, so it is a perfectly well-documented application of the strategic command and control of the Republika Srpska armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the last paragraph, we see that General Tolimir says: "In accordance with the order of the president of Republika Srpska ..." And I won't read it all, but he says: "... you must issue an order to all combat units," and, basically, "to offer protection to UNPROFOR members and civilian Muslims." Then he says: "You must order subordinate units to refrain from destroying civilian targets unless forced to do so because of strong enemy resistance." Then he says: "Ban the torching of residential buildings and treat the civilian population and war prisoners in accordance with Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949." Now, these statements basically -- I'm referring to "you must issue" and "you must order," and "ban the torching," these very definitive statements of General Tolimir, is that -- is he empowered to issue such strong directions to Generals Gvero and Krstic? How would you describe -- where does this fit into the chain of command and the giving of orders?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you're correct in that those are directive in nature. But I would take you to the first line of that particular paragraph: "In accordance with the order of the president of the Republika Srpska ..." In that particular context, these instructions are not going to be read by General Gvero and General Krstic as an order from General Tolimir. They are going to be read as General Tolimir rightfully relaying the orders of the president of the Republika Srpska. So in that particular sense, General Tolimir is acting within the competence placed in him by the president of Republika Srpska to issue these specific orders that the president wants issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, before you put the next question to the witness, I have to take you back to page 33, line 23. I think there is a correction necessary. The witness said. "... and obviously in this situation, the military laid out the case that they had the ability to take the town that the military ..." And now it reads "assistance being offered." I think the witness said "resistance" instead of "assistance," just to have a clear record. The witness is nodding, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in a similar vein, would General Tolimir be within his authority to take orders or receive orders from General Mladic and pass them on, in a directive manner, to subordinate units or other units of the -- or people of the VRS, much like he's done here with President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Not only General Tolimir, but, has become apparent in later documents, General Gvero and other officers engaged in similar practices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And going back briefly to the rules reflecting the Geneva Conventions that were in play in the VRS, as well as your knowledge of the Geneva Conventions, when General Tolimir passes on an order such as this, is he responsible in some way if that order is absolutely illegal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The SFRY regulations on the application of the Law of War, as well as even provisions of the Republika Srpska Criminal Code, lay out the fact that there is not an obligation to follow an order, and in that context I say and to presumably transfer an order as well, when it is viewed at its face as being unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now let's continue in the chronology and go to I believe it's 65 ter 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a document that's a bit of a different animal than what we have been seeing throughout the case. As we see, it's from the Republika Srpska Ministry of Interior, Cabinet of the Minister, with the typed name "Tomislav Kovac" as staff commander. We've now moved on to 10 July, and we see that it's to the commander of the Special Police Brigade and others from Trnovo, Vogosca, Bijeljina, Zvornik, Sarajevo, Jahorina, and it's an order from Kovac. Can you remind us who Kovac was at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my understanding, if I recall correctly, that at this time Kovac is the acting minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I will -- I want to spend some time going over this, but I'll paraphrase. The order is, roughly, an order to take some MUP forces from one area of the battle-field and send them to report to General Krstic in the Srebrenica area on 11 July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you know about this order, why you believe it was issued, and who are these various participants that we see? We've heard your explanation about the Special Police Brigade and the PJP, but can you give us your full explanation of this document? And I'll probably ask you some follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the now change of mission, which will include the physical capture or occupation of Srebrenica, somebody at the highest levels of the Supreme Command has made a decision that in addition to military forces, additional police forces should be engaged in the activities and made available at that particular area. What this document is is to various commanders and police components, directing them to detach several police companies, some of which are engaged in combat operations elsewhere, and to put them under the command of Ljubisa Borovcanin, as the designated commander, and have those forces sent to Srebrenica theatre. And the last -- you know, when they're supposed to arrive. And then the last component is that once they arrive there, Borovcanin, as the unit commander, is to make contact with General Krstic for additional instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber has heard evidence in this case that a Ljubisa Borovcanin was with Zoran Petrovic when he drove by the Kravica warehouse on the 13th of July and filmed bodies in front of the warehouse. Is this the same Borovcanin that's associated with that film footage and commanding the units along the road on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was his position when he was called upon by this order on the 10th to go to General Krstic with these units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: His formal position at the time was as the deputy commander of the Special Police Brigade that was then headquartered in Janca [phoen], Janjac [phoen]. At the time, in addition to his normal deputy commander duties, he was also leading a particular battle group of police companies that were engaged in the Sarajevo battle-front. Most of the units that are designated in this order, in fact, were companies under his command at Sarajevo. So for whatever reason, it was just deemed expedient to leave him in command of those formations and to have those formations go with him to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you -- have you -- do you know under whose command Borovcanin was working at what you've called the Sarajevo battle-front?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under various Republika Srpska laws relating to the use of the police in times of armed conflict, the normal procedure is that when police are fighting as part of military organisations or in the military context of the battle-field, that the police units are placed under the command of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you to repeat the name of the location where the Special Police Brigade was headquartered, if you recall the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the town is called Janjac, or Jajce, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does "Janja" sound familiar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have different versions on the transcript. Please carry on, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So with those -- with the rule or rules you mentioned, which we'll be seeing a bit later, in your view, under whose command was Borovcanin fighting when he was at the Sarajevo front?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it would have been under the military command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you reviewed documents where Mr. Borovcanin was reporting on the battle situation prior -- at the Sarajevo front prior to July 10th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have, but at this juncture I don't recall the details of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the units that were working with him at the Sarajevo front?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that in that same particular area, there was a composite unit of the Drina Corps, named the 4th Drinski Battalion, or Brigade, I think it was, that was also in a location at the same area. But again, even in that particular case, for their day-to-day activities, they would have fallen at the direction of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me go through this a bit. We see number 1 is: "Detach part of the RS MUP forces that are taking part in the operations at the Sarajevo front and send them sometime tomorrow, 11 July, as an independent unit to the Srebrenica sector." I think that's pretty clear on its face. Number 2: "The unit shall consist of the 2nd Special Police Detachment from Sekovici ..." What is that, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of this particular Special Police Brigade, there were a total of, I believe, nine Special Police detachments that were garrisoned in various areas of Republika Srpska. This particular one, the 2nd -- they're alternatively called anti-terrorism units, but this particular one, the 2nd Special Police Detachment, was garrisoned in the town of Sekovici, which is the Drina Corps area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then the next unit is the 1st Company of the PJP of the Zvornik SJB. Now, you talked a bit about this yesterday. What is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As I discussed, the PJP companies are the companies that are made up of, primarily, municipal police officers from a police region, the CSB, and are organised in a number -- in a series of numbered companies. In this particular case, previously, as a result of the requirement for combat activities, police officers from the Zvornik area had already been mobilised in at least the 1st PJP Company and were already actively conducting combat operations in Sarajevo, under the command of Borovcanin. So that is what this particular PJP company reflects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see, in the address, that it's "Commander of the Special Police Brigade, Staff of the Trnovo Police Forces Command." Where does Trnovo fit into this? That's a town we've heard of before in this case.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trnovo is the actual location around Sarajevo. It's actually somewhere between Sarajevo and the Gorazde area, where the police forces, as well as the forces of the 4th Drinski Brigade, were employed in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And continuing on my list or the list: We have now the -- a mixed company of joint Republika Serbian Krajina, Serbian and RS MUP forces. What is that a reference to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that as part of the unit fighting under MUP control in Trnovo, there was a composite group that was comprised of police from the Republika Serb Krajina, which is that independent autonomous country that -- it isn't Republika Srpska, it's further to the west, as well as members of the federal MUP, a small number of those individuals who were part of this composite company who were engaged in combat activities on behalf of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember the common name of any of the Serbian MUP units that were engaged in the Trnovo area in this period before 10 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They referred to themselves as the Skorpions unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Has the investigation revealed any evidence that Serbian MUP units, as described here, actually came with Borovcanin to the Srebrenica area on 11 July, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly do recall that that was something that the investigation looked very deeply into, not necessarily for the ramifications related to Srebrenica, but simply because at that point in time it did have ramifications related to the prosecution of Slobodan Milosevic. So there was, investigatively, a very high priority placed on trying to confirm or deny that this particular federal Yugoslavian MUP organisation went to Srebrenica. And at the time that I departed in October/November 2003, to my knowledge, the investigation had revealed no information which would confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And, lastly, a company from the training camp on Jahorina, what is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Jahorina facility was a police facility near Sarajevo that was used to train newly-recruited or conscripted individuals in the Special Police. In July of 1995, there were a total of two conscript companies that were being trained at the facility at the time. We call them conscripts, in a sense, because many of them were Bosnian Serbs who had been apprehended in Serbia by the Serbian MUP in the previous months and had been returned back to the Republika Srpska so they could be inducted into military or police service. Another name that you will hear associated with these two particular companies is they're referred to as the deserter companies, a reference to the fact that the police officers who are in them were formerly those people who deserted to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in paragraph 5, we see: "On arrival at --" Well, 4, we see the logistics of how and when the units are supposed to get to the area of Bratunac and Sarajevo -- excuse me, and Srebrenica, and it says: "On arrival at his destination, the unit commander ..." And who would the unit commander be in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be Ljubisa Borovcanin, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "... is obliged to make contact with the corps chief of staff, General Krstic." Have you formed an opinion on the command relationship, or lack thereof, between Ljubisa Borovcanin, and his forces mentioned here, and that of the VRS and General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your view on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this order correctly documents the relationship as it was supposed to exist under the applicable Republika Srpska law. When the Special Police unit under the command of Borovcanin arrived, he and that particular unit fell under the control of the VRS. At the time, General Krstic, as the chief of staff and later as the Drina Corps, and as other information bears out in the next several days, the 12th, the 13th, 14th and 15th, you know, it becomes clear that the Special Police unit is taking their orders from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you say "the Special Police unit." Would that include the PJP units and the Jahorina training unit as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, all of these particular units that are associated with Colonel -- at this time, he's still Ljubisa Borovcanin, he's not a colonel yet. But these police units fall under Borovcanin's command, and Borovcanin takes his orders from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you explain your last comment, that he's not a colonel yet?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's in August of 1995, in order to more appropriately align the police and the army in rank structure, that the officers of the -- at least the Special Police Brigade are given military ranks. In the case of Borovcanin, in August of 1995 he is given the appointment of the rank of a colonel, so many of the documents relating to Borovcanin post-July 1995 will refer to him as Colonel Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 54 shall be assigned Exhibit P2516. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we now go to P1618.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This should be a section of the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska referencing various laws. Is that correct, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to it's page 12 in the English, and it's Article 14. In the Serbian -- I'm sorry, I've lost my reference in the Serbian. It's Chapter 4, "The Use of Police Units in Combat Operations," if that would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I'm not mistaken, it's page 5 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much for helping out on that point. I think you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this section, entitled "The Use of Police Units in Combat Operations," was that something that you have referenced in your report and have just spoken about briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we look at Article 14, does that basically - and I won't read all of it - set out what you have said? And just, again, if you can just reiterate it, as you see it, from the language of this law.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It lays out who assigns the police to these combat operations, reflecting that it ultimately is the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, who is President Karadzic. It lays out what orders will be given when this occurs, and lays out conditions of what can and cannot occur, which is important, in a sense, because the police can only be used on tasks that have already been previously agreed to by the army and the Ministry of the Interior. So the army does not have cart blanche to do anything that they want with various police units. They have to employ them within certain previously specified limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in this second paragraph, that says: "Police units shall be under the direct command of a commander who is a member of the Ministry of the Interior." And who would that be, in our situation, related to the 10 July document we just went over?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be Ljubisa Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what about logistic support? We see the last paragraph. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Police forces, as you might expect, do not normally have the complex logistics or the amount of munitions, food, and other things necessary to sustain themselves over a period of days or even weeks in combat operations, so this is an obligation that when police forces are used in military operations, that the Army of the Republika Srpska, you know, incurs the obligation to ensure that they are properly supplied and re-equipped as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And this comment: "... the commander to whom a police unit has been re-subordinated shall provide logistic support," in your view, has Borovcanin's unit been re-subordinated to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Because I note, if we go back to the 10 July document from Tomislav Kovac, there is no reference to the law, there is no mention of the word "re-subordinated." It just -- it says: "Pursuant to the order of the supreme commander of the Republika Srpska Armed Forces," and then it says: "I hereby order:" So can you just briefly -- and, I'm sorry, but I think you're just going to repeat what it is that you base your opinion that Borovcanin and his forces are actually re-subordinated to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, it is a reflection of my view that in the context of military operations, that the relevant commanders and their staff officers are going to operate in compliance with existing law and regulations. It should not have to be stated in an order like Kovac is given where he would have to specify which various acts of Republika Srpska law are applicable and empower him to issue this order. The president of the republic knows what the law is. Minister Kovac knows what the law is. Borovcanin knows what the law is. The army knows what the law is.
